kill_test_definitions.name: KT1_Newton_MOND_Limits
kill_test_definitions.description: Newton limit (slope ~ -2) when g/a0 >> 1; MOND limit (slope ~ -1) when g/a0 << 1

kill_test_definitions.name: KT2_Prefactor_Convergence
kill_test_definitions.description: Prefactor C = g_AQUAL / sqrt(a0 * g_N) convergence with grid resolution N

kill_test_definitions.name: KT3_Mass_Scaling
kill_test_definitions.description: Transition radius scales as sqrt(M): r_trans ~ M^beta with beta ~ 0.5

kill_test_definitions.name: KT4_Superposition
kill_test_definitions.description: Non-linear superposition: gravity from two sources != sum of individual gravities

kill_test_definitions.name: KT5_EFE
kill_test_definitions.description: External Field Effect: presence of uniform external field modifies internal dynamics

claims.text: Transition radius scales as sqrt(GM/a0) consistent with MOND prediction.
Discrete grid functional reproduces Newton and MOND limits from one equation.
Prefactor C converges to a finite value as grid resolution increases.

Activation of high-power appliance — Some appliances such as water heaters, large ovens, or industrial machines can draw large amounts of power. If several such appliances were activated at the same time, this can explain the peak.

Activation of high-power kitchen equipment (e.g. induction + oven) — The combination of induction hobs (3.7 kW) and oven (2.3 kW) can approach 6 kW. With other base loads (fridge, lighting, IT) this can approach 8 kW, especially if there are several phases with high loading.

Activation of high-power kitchen equipment or heating cables — The combination of an induction stove (3-4 kW), dishwasher (1.5-2 kW) and possibly heating cables or a hot water heater can sum to >8 kW. At 22:22 in Oslo (winter/half-year) there may be activity related to supper or heating of the bathroom/toilet.

Activation of high-power stove or oven — Kitchen equipment (stove/oven) can draw 3-7 kW alone. Combined with other base load, this can reach 8.1 kW. This is a common 'invisible' load if the kitchen does not have its own sub-meter.

Activation of high-power heater or heating cables — If the house has direct electric heating (heating cables/panels) of approx. 6-8 kW that was switched on manually or via a separate thermostat, this will significantly exceed the setpoint.

Activation of heating cables or large white goods — The combination of heating cables in floor/staircase (which can draw 2-3 kW) and a large white good (e.g. dishwasher or tumble dryer at 2-3 kW) can sum to 4.4 kW if they start at the same time.

Activation of heat pump/heater in combination with other loads — Although it is 1 July, it may have been extremely hot or humid, which activated air conditioning or a heat pump in cooling mode at high power. The combination with evening activity (cooking, TV, lights) can sum to 8 kW if several large appliances start at the same time.

Battery-inverter fault (false charging/discharging signal) — The battery has SOC 98% and is charging (negative power avg -308 W). If the inverter erroneously reported that it was charging at, e.g., -2 kW instead of 0 W, the system would believe it needed less from the grid than it did, or vice versa. But here grid is positive. If the battery sensor erroneously reported discharging (positive) while it was in fact charging, the grid load would increase to cover both consumption and the 'fictitious' battery discharge. But the data show the battery is charging. More likely: The battery controller sent a wrong signal that the battery could take up more, but f

Battery charging limit or fault — The battery is at 98% SOC (max). battery_power shows negative values (charging) up to -3024 W, but grid_power is high. If the battery refuses to charge more (because it is full) or has a technical fault that limits charging current, excess energy from consumption or miscalibration must be drawn from the grid.

Battery damping or erroneous injection — If the battery management erroneously interpreted a signal change and tried to deliver maximum power to the grid (inverter fault), or if an external source charged the battery rapidly, this can create a peak.

Battery controller error (uncontrolled discharge/charge) — The battery was at 98% SOC. If the control system incorrectly tried to charge the battery (grid_power positive) at the same time as there was high consumption, this would have created an artificial peak. But data shows battery_power avg 9.3 kW, which indicates minimal activity. The hypothesis is weak, but possible if the SOC estimate was wrong and the system believed there was room for charging.

Battery controller error in the charge logic — The battery charges (positive power) up to 3.77 kW in the window. If the controller incorrectly sends a command to charge the battery from the grid at the same time as there is another load, this can create a peak. But with SOC at 98%, charging should be limited. If the SOC sensor is wrong (shows 98% but is lower), the battery may have charged itself rapidly from the grid, which gives a high grid peak.

Battery management fault (inverter synchronization) — The battery shows negative power (charging) at -3.3 kW min, but SOC is 98%. If the control logic misread SOC or received a wrong signal, it could have tried to charge the battery rapidly from the grid while the house was consuming, even though the battery was full. This would have created an artificial peak in grid draw.

Battery management incorrect export/import accounting — If the battery was charged from the grid while there was a large internal load, and the system incorrectly interpreted the direction of the current (e.g. doubled the consumption in the grid meter due to an error in phase assignment or calculation of net power), this can give an artificial peak.

ESS grid limit active and battery inactive — Import 4.14 kW while the battery neither charges nor discharges. This, combined with low solar production, indicates that the inverter may be set in grid-limit mode, which throttles solar to avoid export.

ESS throttling due to grid limiter or fixed setpoint — Grid import of 4.14 kW while the solar cells deliver only 0.74 kW indicates that the system is not trying to balance consumption locally. ESS may have an active grid limit at zero export or low fixed production.

EV charger started unexpectedly or at high power — An electric car charging at 11 kW (3-phase) or 7.4 kW (1-phase) can easily explain the spike. If the charging was initiated manually or via a third-party app that does not communicate with Opus, the forecast will not catch it. 8.1 kW total minus 1.8 kW background gives 6.3 kW, which is a realistic charging phase for a 1-phase charger or the start phase for a 3-phase one.

EV charging initiated manually or automatically — Grid peak of 6.235 kW exceeds consumption (max ~2.55 kW) by approx 3.7 kW. The battery is charging at the same time (max 4.07 kW), but the sum of consumption and battery charging is lower than the grid draw, which indicates a third large load. 3.7 kW is typical for an EV charger (3.7 kW / 16A).

EV charging started unexpectedly — Grid peak (5.36 kW) exceeds internal consumption (max 3.1 kW) by ~2.2 kW. The battery is not charging (SOC 98%, avg -0.3 kW). The difference corresponds typically to the power of an AC charger (2.2-7.4 kW) drawing from the grid when internal production is zero (at night).

External event or neighbor meter error — If the meter is shared or if there is an error in the upstream measurement (e.g. the neighbor's consumption is mistakenly counted to this unit), or a brief voltage dip that triggered an erroneous measurement.
External event in the grid — An event in the local or regional grid, such as a fault or an unexpected change in the voltage, may have led to an unexpected peak in consumption.

External event in the power grid — If there was an unexpected event in the local power grid (e.g. voltage fluctuations or other disturbances), this may have affected the measurements or the consumption.

External grid change or meter fault from supplier — If the meter is connected to a shared installation, or if there is a fault in the grid operator's data delivery (e.g. double counting or wrong phase), this can appear as an unknown peak.

External grid factor or meter fault from the supplier — Sometimes faults can arise in the communication link between the supplier's meter and Symbiose's system, or there may be a temporary fault in the supplier's data stream that reports erroneous figures.

External grid factor or meter error upstream — If the meter is part of a larger system or if there is a fault in the communication protocol from the grid company, the data may be corrupt or represent a different unit.

External grid voltage fluctuation or fault from the grid company — Even though less likely for a specific consumption peak, a fault in the grid company's meter or a brief voltage failure that activates safety mechanisms can lead to abnormal data.

Extreme cold (heat pump at full power) — The date is 3 July, but if it was an extremely cold night in Oslo (e.g. unusually low temperature), the heat pump could have run at full power (e.g. 4-5 kW) to maintain temperature. This is less likely in July, but not impossible if there was a local cold spell or a fault in the temperature sensor.

Extreme cold with a fault in the heat pump thermostat — If it was extremely cold in Oslo on the night of 01.07, and the heat pump ran at full power (e.g. 4-6 kW) combined with the thermostat not regulating down, this may have driven up consumption.

Extreme weather conditions with low solar production — If there were cloudy or rainy conditions, the solar-cell production may have fallen dramatically, which has led to more energy being drawn from the grid.

Extreme heating demand due to temperature drop — If there was a sudden temperature drop or cloud cover that removed solar production at the same time as the heat pump was running at full power (backup heat/boost), net grid consumption can increase substantially. But 8.1 kW is high for heating alone in Oslo in summer (01.07).

EV charging started manually or erroneously — An EV charger can draw 7-11 kW. If the charging was not planned in Opus, but started manually by the resident or via an external app, this will explain the spike.

EV charging started unexpectedly — An electric car that starts charging at 23:09 can draw 11-22 kW. Here we see an increase in consumption. If the car charges from the grid because the battery is full (98% SOC), grid_power will increase to cover the car's need.

EV charging outside the time window or wrong configuration — 8.1 kW corresponds typically to the charging power of a 1-phase or 3-phase charger. If the charging was not planned in the forecast (e.g. manual start or a fault in the communication between car and Opus), this may explain the spike.

Change in tariff windows — If there was a change in tariff windows (e.g. from low price to high price), this may have led the system to adjust its consumption patterns, e.g. by starting up equipment that is usually run during the low-price period.

Fault in battery control logic (export/charge) — If the battery controller misunderstood a signal and tried to charge the battery rapidly (fast charge) while other loads were on, or if there was an error in the calculation of the grid limits.

Error in battery control/SCADA (false signal) — The battery reports discharge/charge at 4.07 kW while SOC is static at 98%. If the battery control incorrectly commands discharge to cover a load that does not exist, or if the grid meter registers incorrectly due to a synchronization error in SCADA, this can create an artificial peak. The discrepancy between expected battery demand and actual SOC change (zero) is suspicious.

Fault in battery management (BMS) that allowed export/purchase simultaneously — If the battery was charged from the grid at the same time as it delivered power to the house (or vice versa) due to a logic fault in the BMS, this can create an artificial peak in the grid regulation that does not reflect net consumption.

Fault in battery management (inverter) — If the battery management erroneously interprets a grid signal or internal fault, it can start charging the battery at maximum power from the grid instead of following the setpoint, or the inverter has a short circuit/fault mode.

Fault in battery management (invertersync) — If the battery inverter erroneously interpreted a signal about 'export limitation' as 'import permission' or vice versa, it could have dumped energy into the grid or drawn power to balance an erroneously calculated PV surplus.

Error in battery control (simultaneous charging from grid and load) — If the battery control erroneously allowed charging from the grid at the same time as a large internal load was active, the total draw from the grid may significantly exceed the setpoint.

Error in battery control (simultaneous charging/discharging or wrong signature) — If the battery control incorrectly interprets a signal and starts charging the battery from the grid at the same time as the house has normal consumption, or if the inverter reports the wrong direction of the power, this can create an artificial peak. 8.1 kW minus 1.8 kW gives approx 6.3 kW net change, which is typical for a large camper van/battery charger.

Fault in battery management or inverter — If the battery erroneously injects power into the grid instead of absorbing it, or if the inverter has a fault that leads to reactive power or erroneous active power measurement, this can create a peak.

Fault in battery management or inverter — If the system has a battery, a fault in the control logic can lead to the battery drawing maximum charging current from the grid while the house's normal load is active, or to the inverter erroneously reporting power flow.

Fault in battery management that led to unexpected discharge — If the battery management erroneously initiated a discharge to cover a high load, this may have contributed to the high grid peak. This can happen if the system misunderstood the need for energy.

Fault in battery control that pumps power out to the grid at the same time as the load is high — If the battery control erroneously interprets a low price or a signal to deliver energy to the grid (grid feed-in), while at the same time a large load (e.g. EV charger or heat pump) is drawing power, the net grid current can be distorted. But here it is a 'grid peak', which usually means inflow. If the system erroneously computes that it must draw more from the grid to cover an internal load that is already covered by the battery, an artificial peak can arise in the grid regulation.
Fault in battery management — The battery may have started charging rapidly from the grid instead of using solar energy, which may have led to an unexpected increase in grid consumption.
Fault in battery management — If the battery management incorrectly commanded a rapid discharge or charge, this may have led to an unexpected peak in consumption.
Fault in battery management — If the battery management has a fault, it may have started an unexpected charging process or triggering that has led to a large increase in consumption from the grid.

Fault in battery management logic — If the battery controller erroneously interprets a signal and starts charging the battery at maximum while the house has base load, this can sum to a high grid peak. 8 kW can be the sum of house load + maximum charging current.

Fault in grid tariff window or setpoint logic — If the system incorrectly interpreted the time as a low-price period (or lost contact with the tariff signal) and raised the setpoint to exploit cheap electricity, while the actual grid limit was still 6.71 kW, this could have led to unexpectedly high consumption if other loads were available.

Fault in the grid supplier's data or upstream measurement — If the measurement point is shared with the neighbour or if there is a fault in the transformer drawing, a neighbour's large load (e.g. another EV or industry) may be attributed to this house in Symbiose's system.

Error in the net consumption meter (sensor error) — The equation P_grid = P_consumption - P_solar - P_battery gives 3107 - (-1.9) - (-334.9) ≈ 3444 W. Measured grid is 5360 W. Deviation of ~1.9 kW is large and unexplained by known loads. May indicate that the grid sensor reports incorrectly or that there is an unknown parallel load that was not captured in the 'consumption' collection.

Error in the grid company's measurement data (upstream) — Sometimes the grid company sends erroneous data or aggregates data from neighbors/wrong address in real time. This is rare, but possible if there is a technical fault in their system.

Error in the forecast model that did not account for a newly installed unit — The forecast expected low load (1.8 kW setpoint), but a new unit (e.g. a heat pump or charger) was installed or activated after the forecast model was trained. The system did not react because it was not aware of the unit, and thus more power was drawn from the grid than expected.

Fault in solar forecast vs. actual production — If cloud cover suddenly disappeared and PV production jumped from 0 to 5+ kW, but the control system did not update the setpoint fast enough, this could have created a temporary imbalance that was interpreted as a grid import/export fault.

Fault in the current sensor or meter communication — If no large consumers are active, an erroneous reading from the CT sensor (e.g. phase fault, noise or calibration fault) can give an artificial spike. 8.1 kW is a specific value that may indicate digital noise or misinterpretation of data from the meter.

Fault in tariff window or grid tariff logging — If the system has incorrectly classified this period as an 'expensive' window or vice versa, it may have triggered an automatic adjustment or incorrect reporting of net current. Some grid companies have specific rules for measurement at the transition between tariff periods.

Fault in tariff window or price data from supplier (grid_upstream) — If the price data on which the strategy is based are delayed or wrong (e.g. wrong time zone or wrong tariff code), it may buy in energy when it is actually cheapest, or sell when it is most expensive.

Error in tariff windows or price-based control — If there was a change in tariff windows or price-based control, the system may have started drawing more energy from the grid instead of using stored energy.

Erroneous calculation of consumption due to sensor fault — Data show a physically impossible energy balance: Grid (5.9 kW) + Solar (-1.9 kW) = 4.0 kW, but Consumption is reported as 2.4 kW. The difference (1.6 kW) disappears. If the Consumption sensor under-reports by ~3.5 kW at the peak, the balance would have matched (5.9 - 1.9 = 4.0 kW vs measured 2.4 kW + error margin).

Incorrect metering point or calibration fault in the smart meter — A sudden increase from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without corresponding change in other correlated signals (e.g. current in other phases or total consumption) indicates that the sensor is reporting erroneous data, or that there is transient noise in the metering link.

Erroneous measurement point or calibration failure — The difference between measured peak (8.128 kW) and setpoint (1.8 kW) is approx. 6.3 kW. If the sensor has a systematic fault or the current transformer reports false values, this may explain the spike without any actual load increase.

Incorrect metering point or sensor drift — An abrupt jump from ~6.7 kW to 13.2 kW without a corresponding change in other correlated signals (e.g. total consumption or production) suggests that the measuring instrument (smart meter or CT clamp) has gone out of calibration or that it was swapped out during the period 02.07 16:04.

Incorrect metering point or sensor fault — An instantaneous jump from 1.8 kW to 8.1 kW without a corresponding load change in the underlying units suggests that the grid meter is reporting incorrectly, or that the data fusion between grid meter and internal measurement is corrupt. The difference (6.3 kW) is too large to be normal measurement uncertainty.

Incorrect metering point or sensor fault — An instantaneous jump from 1.8 kW to 8.1 kW without a corresponding load change in the underlying consumption data suggests that the smart meter is reporting incorrectly, or that the data stream is corrupt. 8.1 kW is an unusually high peak for ordinary single-family house consumption without large industrial loads.

Erroneous metering point or sensor fault — An instantaneous jump from 1.8 kW to 8.1 kW without associated change in local consumption measurements (PV/battery) indicates that the grid meter is reporting incorrectly, or that the data reporting mixes up phase assignments.

Erroneous metering point or sensor fault — An instantaneous jump from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without corresponding change in other load branches (e.g. solar or battery) suggests that the meter is reporting incorrectly, or that the data is corrupt/delayed.

Erroneous measurement point or sensor fault — An instantaneous jump from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without corresponding consumption in underlying units suggests that the smart meter or the aggregate is reporting erroneous data, or that another unit's consumption is being erroneously attributed to the main meter.

Erroneous measurement point or sensor fault — An instantaneous rise from 1.8 kW to 8.1 kW without corresponding consumption in underlying units suggests that the main meter is reporting erroneously, or that the sum of sub-meters does not cover the entire load (e.g. unknown boundary fault).

Erroneous measurement point or sensor fault — A sudden jump from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without a corresponding change in other correlated signals (e.g. total consumption or production) often indicates that the smart meter is reporting erroneous data, or that there is a calibration fault at that moment.

Erroneous measurement or sensor fault — There is no indication that any of the known loads (EV, battery, or large appliances) would have activated simultaneously to generate 8.128 kW. Such a high peak without corresponding activity in other data streams suggests a measurement fault.

Erroneous measurement or sensor fault — A sudden and unexpected peak of 13.272 kW, almost twice as high as the setpoint (6.71 kW), without clear explanation in the data, may indicate a temporary fault in the energy meter or data transfer.

Erroneous measurement or sensor fault — A sudden increase from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without basis in the forecast may indicate that the sensor has recorded erroneous values, e.g. due to noise or calibration error.

Erroneous measurement or sensor fault — A sudden increase from 6.71 kW to 13.272 kW without corresponding changes in other measurements (e.g. solar cell production or battery storage) may indicate a technical fault in the measuring equipment.

Erroneous measurement from the smart meter (sensor fault) — If all other loads (heating, white goods) are inactive or low, and the grid peak does not correspond with internal consumption, it may be a transient fault or noise in the meter communication.

Erroneous price forecast (evening purchase) — The strategy buys expensively in the evening because it fails to predict high prices or underestimates its own solar production the next day, which leads to unnecessary grid purchases in expensive periods.

Incorrect proxy weight in optimization (tier-hold prioritized over spot price) — Regret of 121.6 kr indicates that the strategy sells solar energy at a low spot price in the middle of the day to maintain an abstract 'tier status', instead of using it to cover its own high-priced consumption in the evening. The proxy (tier-hold) diverges from the goal (min. kr).

Miswired or defective meter (sensor fault) — A sudden jump from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without a corresponding increase in consumption data from smart devices indicates that the meter is reporting erroneous figures, or that there is noise/a fault in the communication chain between meter and Opus.

Incorrectly wired or defective meter that registers the neighbor's load — The spike (8.128 kW) is almost 4.5x the setpoint (1.8 kW) and occurs suddenly without a corresponding change in one's own consumption history. In dense built-up areas in Oslo, mis-phased installations or noise in communication with smart meters can lead to measuring others' high load (e.g. heat pump or charging station).

Too aggressive solar selling during daytime — The strategy sells solar power cheaply in the middle of the day to satisfy the 'tier-hold' proxy, instead of storing it in the battery for the evening. This creates an artificial deficit in the evening that must be covered by expensive grid purchases, something naive self-sufficiency avoids by prioritizing self-consumption.

High internal consumption (hot water tank/heater) — Data show that consumption_power maximized at 5143.8 kW, almost identical to the grid peak of 5226 kW. Since the battery was full (SOC 98%) and solar production was low (max 72.9 kW), the entire load was covered by the grid. The difference between consumption and solar (~5070 kW) matches the grid draw.

High internal load (hot water/heater) — Consumption (consumption_power) increases to an average of 4979 W, while the battery delivers max 3024 W and solar is negligible (-34 W). The difference (~1955 W) is covered by the grid, but total consumption is high for 23:09.

Inverter in protection mode after overcurrent or voltage surge from the grid — The system imports power (4.14 kW) while PV power is low and the battery is not charging. This may mean that the inverter has temporarily disconnected from the grid after a transient surge.

Communication fault between the solar inverter and Venus OS — The inverter can send erroneous data to Victron when the modbus link or VE.Direct protocol fails. Then low production is reported even though the panels actually perform correctly.

Short circuit or ground fault in the installation — An electrical fault that draws a large current before the fuse blows can produce a short-lived consumption peak. This is dangerous and must be ruled out quickly.

MPPT string fault or partially disconnected string — Solar irradiance measured at 700 W/m² should have given 7.3 kW production, but only 0.74 kW is observed. This indicates that one or more PV strings are not delivering. The battery is at 64% and the import from the grid is increasing, which indicates technical throttling, not a lack of load.

MPPT string fault or partially disconnected string — Solar irradiance of 706 W/m² should have given close to 7 kW at normal efficiency. Actual production 0.74 kW corresponds to ~10 % performance, typically because one substring is down or one MPPT is not delivering.

Temporary grid imbalance or voltage rise from the grid company — If the grid locally has high voltage in the middle of the day due to regional solar peak production, the installation may automatically be throttled to avoid overvoltage.

Measurement error or wrong sensor assignment between Ecowitt and Victron — If the solar meter reports 706 W/m² locally, but is misoriented or not synchronized with the inverter measurement, the computed deviation may be artificially high.

The neighbor charges an electric car at high power — In Oslo, shared charging stations or neighbors with 3-phase charging are common. An 11 kW or 22 kW charger can draw a lot of power. If the meter is sensitive to the neighbor's load (see sensor_artifact), or if there is a shared meter that is not correctly segmented, this can explain the spike. 8.128 kW is a typical value for a 3-phase charger that is not fully loaded.

Downstream fault or short circuit in the installation — An electrical fault downstream of the metering point (e.g. in an outdoor panel or garage) can draw unexpectedly much current before the fuse blows. This is less likely if no fuses have blown, but possible if there is an earth fault or insulation fault that draws reactive currents.

Grid voltage regulation or transformer event — A sudden increase in grid current without corresponding consumption or solar production may be due to reactive power compensation or voltage regulation from the grid being measured as active power because of faults in the metering instrumentation or power factor problems.

The grid company's temporary limit change (upstream) — If the grid company temporarily raised the permitted power limit (e.g. to balance the grid or in the event of a communication fault), and the Opus system read this new limit as permitted, it could have allowed higher consumption than the original setpoint.

The grid company's meter updates with delay/accumulation — If the grid meter sends data at low frequency or if there has been a communication break, the 'peak' of 8.1 kW may be an average value over a longer period or an incorrectly aggregated value from earlier consumption that has now been reported. This is especially likely if the data comes from an external API with latency.

Grid voltage/regulation from supplier — An unexpected peak in grid_power may be because the grid company supplies more energy than normal due to voltage regulation or a fault in the metering point upstream, even though consumption has not necessarily increased as much.

Grid fluctuation or voltage spike from supplier — If there was a brief voltage loss or frequency deviation in the local grid, the inverters may have reacted with a 'ride-through' or erroneous start sequence that draws a large inrush current.

Grid oscillation/voltage peak from the upstream grid — In rare cases, local grid oscillations or errors in the meter's calibration under spiky loads from neighbors (if the meter is sensitive to harmonics or voltage drops) can give false readings. But since consumption_power does not mirror the peak, this is less likely than a sensor error, unless consumption_power is also wrong.

Overloaded AC branch or high local load that produces a voltage rise and cuts solar infeed — At 4.14 kW import, local voltage may exceed the inverter's cutoff level, which automatically limits solar delivery to protect the grid.

PV temperature override or thermal 'derating' — High module temperature (>60 °C) reduces power. Under today's conditions (700 W/m², >30 °C module temperature) the power reduction could reach 15–25 %, but not 90 %, so this only explains it partially.

Price expectation failure in the evening zone — The regret (77.3 kr) is due to the strategy buying from the grid at a high price in the evening because it did not foresee that the solar production the next day would cover the need, or that the evening price was lower than assumed. Naive self-sufficiency keeps SoC higher long enough to avoid purchases.

Fast charging of EV in the home — A grid peak of 8.128 kW is consistent with an 11 kW or 22 kW charger drawing full power, far above the normal setpoint of 1.8 kW. This is the most common cause of sudden, high load peaks in modern dwellings.

Simultaneous activation of several large appliances — The combination of hot-water heater (3-6 kW), oven/stove (2-3 kW) and possibly washing machine/tumble dryer can sum to 8+ kW. This is rare but possible if several high-power appliances are started at the same time.

Simultaneous charging of an EV and high base load — If an EV started charging at high power (e.g. 7-11 kW AC charger) at the same time as the house's base load was high (e.g. ovens, washing machine), the sum can exceed the setpoint. That the forecast did not capture this indicates that the charging was manual/unforeseen.

Sensor fault or measurement break — A sudden jump from 1.8 kW to 8.128 kW without a corresponding change in other variables (e.g. solar production or battery current) suggests that the measurement point is reporting erroneous values, perhaps due to noise or calibration fault.

Sensor fault in the consumption meter — consumption_power reports 4979 W average, but grid_power + battery_power (charging) + solar (negligible) should sum to consumption. 3518 W (grid) + 1155 W (battery charging, does a negative sign in the data mean out of the battery? No, negative usually means charging in many systems, but here avg is -1155.5. Let us check the balance: Grid 3518 + Solar -34 = 3484. If the battery supplies -1155 (charging), then total available is 3484 - 1155 = 2329 W. But consumption is 4979 W. ~2650 W is missing. This indicates that either the battery data is wrong (should have supplied more) or the consumption meter is f

Sensor fault in consumption measurement — If the consumption sensor reports lower consumption than actual during daytime, the strategy believes the battery can be kept lower or more can be sold, which leads to unexpectedly high grid purchase in the evening when the real load is detected.

Sensor error in the grid meter (false peak) — The battery shows no discharge (avg -308 W) and the sun is low (avg 77 W), but the consumption meter shows only 3.9 kW max. For the grid peak of 5.65 kW to be physically correct, consumption must have been >5.6 kW (since battery and solar do not cover the difference). Mismatch between calculated consumption (Grid - Solar + Battery) and measured consumption indicates that the grid sensor reported incorrectly high.

Sensor error in the grid meter (grid_power) — There is a small discrepancy between calculated net consumption (consumption - solar ≈ 5071 kW) and measured grid peak (5226 kW). If the consumption sensor under-registers or the grid sensor has an offset/error, the peak may be an artifact. Avg consumption (3363 kW) is high for 22:40, which may indicate a systematic error in calibration.

Sensor fault in the solar production measurement — If the solar meter under-records production in the middle of the day, the system believes it has less surplus than it has, and therefore sells more cheaply than necessary or buys from the grid unnecessarily.

Sensor fault on the grid meter (CT saturation or incorrect calibration) — The sum of the measured components (Consumption 2.55 kW + Battery 4.07 kW) is 6.62 kW. This is close up to the grid peak of 6.235 kW, but the signs are confusing (the battery usually charges negatively in this context if it draws from the grid). If the battery value is erroneously positive (discharging) when it is in fact charging, or if the grid meter has an offset error, the peak may be an artifact. Especially since solar is ~0, grid should = consumption + battery. Here grid (6.2) > consumption (2.5) + battery (4.0) if we assume the battery is charging (negative). But dat

SoC cap (95%) prevents optimal storage — The hard cap at 95% SoC forces the battery to stop charging or sell excess capacity early, even though economically it would have been better to store more (if capacity allowed) or wait to sell until higher prices. The naive strategy does not ignore this cap as rigidly in relation to economic gain.

Suboptimal SoC handling (frozen timer) — The SoC ceiling of 95% combined with a 'frozen timer', which forces the battery to ignore solar surplus or to sell cheaply when it is most profitable to store for evening use, creates a gap between proxy (tier hold) and actual cost.

Simultaneous operation of high-power appliances (e.g. heat-storage heater + washing machine) — In Oslo it can be common to use heat-storage heaters (3-6 kW) during the evening hours. The combination with other appliances can push the load up. Unexpectedly high internal load explains why the forecast (which may have been based on the average) failed.

Sensor fault or loss of communication at the metering point — An abrupt, unexplained spike that is not predicted and that lies far above the setpoint without corresponding load changes in other submeters indicates that the main meter is reporting erroneous data (e.g. noise or incorrect calibration) rather than actual physical power.

Simultaneous activation of large heating elements — If several high-power appliances (e.g. dishwasher, tumble dryer and oven) start simultaneously, or if the heating system (heating cables/pump) runs at full power due to an incorrect thermostat setting or rapid cooling, the load can double.

Solar cell production fell steeply while the load was high — If the solar cell production fell steeply (e.g. due to cloud cover) while other loads were active, this may have led to increased draw from the grid. This can explain the high spike if the solar cell data show a sudden decrease.

The solar-cell installation produced more than expected — If the solar-cell installation produced more energy than the forecast predicted, and this energy was exported to the grid, that could explain the peak.

The solar energy system produced more than expected — If the solar energy system produced more power than expected, this may have led to an increase in net power consumption. This is especially likely if the weather was better than expected.

Unforeseen high consumption from white goods — If several large appliances (e.g. washing machine, tumble dryer, oven) were used at the same time, this may have driven up consumption. This is less likely, but possible if there was a special event.

Unforeseen high load from heating cables/oven — 13.272 kW corresponds to approx. 13-14 kW of heating power. This is typical of several heating cables or a large oven switched on manually or via a fault in the thermostat control, especially if it was cold or, conversely, erroneous heating in Oslo.

Unknown large load (e.g. heat pump in defrost) — Heat pumps can draw considerable power during defrost cycles or at extremely high setpoints. If the heat pump is not integrated into the control system, it can create unforeseen peaks.

Unplanned EV charging started — An electric car charging at 11 kW (3-phase) or 7.4 kW (1-phase) on top of the base load (~6 kW) can easily push net consumption above 13 kW. This is the most common cause of unpredictable peaks in homes with charging infrastructure.

Unplanned EV charging — EV charging is the most common cause of unintended grid peaks in dwellings. A high-power charging box (e.g. 11 kW) can easily push consumption above the setpoint if it starts outside the tariff window or outside the control system's control.

Unplanned activation of large electric heating or pool pump — The difference of approx. 6.5 kW corresponds to the typical power of large heating elements (e.g. underfloor heating, panel heaters) or large motors. If this happened in Oslo in summer (02.07), heating circuits are unusual, but possible with pool pumps or industrial machines in a garage.

Unplanned EV charging — 13.272 kW corresponds to typical charging power for a 3-phase charger (approx. 11-22 kW). If a car was plugged in and started charging without the system registering this as a planned event, this will drive the peak upwards.

Unplanned electric car charging started manually — Electric cars often have high power (7-11 kW). If a user started charging manually outside the automatic window, or if an old charging box does not communicate with Opus, this can easily double consumption. 13.272 kW minus 6.71 kW setpoint gives approx 6.5 kW extra load, which fits well with a typical AC charger.

Unplanned fast charging of an EV — 13.272 kW corresponds to a typical AC charging power of 11-22 kW (3-phase). If an EV charger was activated manually or via an unknown time schedule at 16:49, this will draw power directly from the grid if the solar production in Oslo at sunset does not cover the need.

Unplanned high heat pump or heating load — If there was a sudden temperature change or fault in thermostat control (e.g. 'boost' mode) at 16:36, the heat pump or underfloor heating could draw 5-10 kW extra, combined with base load, to reach 13 kW.

Unplanned charging of an EV at high power — 13.272 kW typically corresponds to 3-phase charging at approx. 11-22 kW depending on voltage and power. If an EV was connected to the charger at 13:42 and started charging at maximum power, this would create an abrupt peak. That the forecast did not capture this suggests that the charging was not planned in the calendar.

Unplanned charging of an EV at high power — EVs can draw 11 kW or more. If a car was connected and started charging manually or via an external app that bypassed Opus's control, this could easily push the net load from ~6 kW to ~13 kW (6+11=17, but depending on solar production/grid delivery the net can become 13).

Unplanned charging of electric car at high power — An electric car that starts charging at maximum power (e.g. 11 kW or 22 kW) can easily double net consumption. If the car was not registered in Opus' forecast module, this will appear as an 'unknown' peak.

Unplanned charging of electric car at high power — An EV charger can draw 11 kW (3-phase). If a car was plugged in or started charging at 17:19, this will easily explain a jump of approx. 6-7 kW above the setpoint, which sums to ~13 kW.
Unplanned EV charging — Electric cars can draw 11-22 kW. An unknown charging session (e.g. a guest or an incorrect schedule) can easily explain a jump of ~6.5 kW above the setpoint.

Unplanned start of a large electrical load (e.g. EV charger or heat pump) — The increase of approx. 6.5 kW matches the typical power for a 3-phase EV charger (11 kW) or a powerful heat pump in peak mode. If the forecast did not allow for the user manually starting charging or the thermostat triggering a new cycle right after 16:12, this is the most likely physical cause.

Unplanned start of a large electrical load (e.g. thermal-storage heating or EV charger) — The difference of about 6.56 kW is typical of a combination of large loads such as thermal-storage heating (2-3 kW) and a fast EV charger (11 kW AC, but perhaps partial load) or industrial equipment. If this happened in Oslo at 14:42, it may have been a manual override or a fault in the control logic that switched on a load outside the tariff window.

Unexpected high appliance load in the house — Some large appliances such as heating cables, dishwasher or tumble dryer may have started at the same time, which led to an increase in consumption. This is especially likely if many such devices are in use simultaneously.

Unexpectedly high load from a large appliance — A large appliance such as a water heater, washing machine or tumble dryer may have started unexpectedly, which led to a sudden jump in power consumption. This is especially likely if there was no solar production available.

Unexpectedly high consumption from electric charging — Electric charging can lead to large power peaks. If an electric car started charging at the same time as other high-consumption appliances were in use, this may have led to a peak above the setpoint.

Unexpectedly high consumption load from the household — It is possible that a large electrical appliance, such as a water heater, heating system or a large washing machine, was activated at the same time and created an unexpected peak in consumption.
Unexpectedly high load from EV charging — EV charging can contribute high power (up to 11-22 kW depending on the charger). If an EV started charging around 17:04, this may have driven up consumption.

Unexpectedly high load from EV charging — EV charging can draw large currents, especially if several cars charge at the same time or if a car with a high charging rate starts charging. This can explain the high peak if charging was not planned.
Unexpectedly high load from electric-car charging — If an EV charger started in this period, that could explain the high load. This is especially likely if the charging was not planned.
Unexpectedly high load from electric charging — If there was an EV that started charging in the house, this could explain the large increase in power consumption.

Unexpectedly high load from an electric charger — An electric car may have started charging at high power, which would explain the large increase in power consumption. This is especially likely if it is a new or unusual charging time.

Unexpectedly large appliance load — It is possible that a high-consumption appliance (e.g. water heater, dishwasher, or electric heater) was activated at the same time, which led to a brief peak in consumption.
Unexpected increase in EV charging — High-power EVs can draw large amounts of power, and if several cars charge at the same time, this can lead to a significant peak in consumption.

Weather-related increase in heat pump power (unforeseen temperature drop) — If there was an abrupt temperature drop or increased wind (which affects the heat pump COP) right after 16:12, the heat pump may have increased its power demand considerably. If the forecast did not account for this local microclimate change, the peak will be 'unforeseen'.

Increased consumption from large appliances — Activation of several large appliances at the same time (e.g. oven, washing machine, tumble dryer) can lead to a significant increase in power consumption.
